reason: Survives on wording, with a locator to tighten. The named Knopf and Faber texts are lending-only on archive.org (fulltext search refused), so the page itself was not opened. But the archive.org search-inside index returns the same two lines, in the same words, from about a dozen printed books that quote Markings and credit the Knopf or Faber translation: Stolpe, Dag Hammarskjöld: A Spiritual Portrait (set with a slash break, For all that has been—Thanks!/ To all that shall be—Yes!); McClendon, Biography as Theology, cited to p. 89; Time to Live, Time to Die; Dunne, A Vision Quest; The Little Book of Prayers, whose acknowledgements credit Alfred A. Knopf and Faber and Faber for Markings. Staalne (Integral Review 7:2) prints the whole entry from the Ballantine reprint at p. 74 and calls it the first entry of 1953; it opens with a first line, Night is drawing nigh, which the quotation leaves out, and so the cut starts at a line head. Wording and the two-line setting agree across every source, and the Swedish (För allt som varit / Tack) matches. Auden’s Markings is criticised as a free translation, but the rule asks only that the wording exist in the named translation, and it does. There are two blemishes, and neither is fatal. (1) The locator: 1953 on its own reads as a date, so it should say the first entry of the 1953 section. The p. 89 is supported by two independent citers but no edition is named, so leave it out. (2) Typography: most clean scans set the dash closed up (been—Thanks!), and the house style elsewhere (03-fict-04) uses closed dashes, so prefer For all that has been—Thanks! / To all that shall be—Yes! The spaced dashes are not the wording, but they are probably not the edition’s setting either. shipped.js: not shipped, no near match, Hammarskjöld 2 of 3 (months 7 and 9), so this line brings him to 3 of 3; not banned. Not on the misattribution list. Diary is the right form. Gratitude and assent to what is coming: squarely November.
betterCitation: Dag Hammarskjöld, Markings, 1953, the section’s first entry (trans. Leif Sjöberg and W. H. Auden, Knopf, 1964)
